chapters.title: October 20, 1771
paragraphs: We arrived here yesterday. The ambassador is unwell and will keep to his rooms for a few days; if only he weren't so peevish, all would be well. I see, I see all too clearly, that fate has hard trials in store for me. But courage! A light heart can bear anything. A light heart? It makes me laugh to see the word come from my pen. Oh, a little more lightness of heart would make me the happiest man under the sun. What! Where others, with their scrap of strength and talent, strut about in front of me in smug self-satisfaction, am I to despair of my own gifts, my own powers? Good God, who gave me all of this — why didn't you keep half of it back and give me self-assurance and contentment instead?

Patience, patience — it will get better. For I tell you, dear friend, you were right. Ever since I've been knocking about among people day after day, seeing what they do and how they go about it, I get on far better with myself. Surely, since we're so made that we measure everything against ourselves and ourselves against everything, our happiness or misery lies in the things we set ourselves beside — and so nothing is more dangerous than solitude. Our imagination, driven by nature to rise, and fed by the fantastic images of poetry, shapes a whole ladder of beings above us, every one of them greater than ourselves, every one more complete. And it's all perfectly natural. We feel so often how much we lack, and what we lack seems to be just what someone else has — to whom we then hand over everything we ourselves possess, and a certain ideal contentment on top of it. And so the happy man stands there, finished and complete — a creature of our own making.

On the other hand, when, for all our weakness and toil, we just keep plodding steadily ahead, we often find that with all our drifting and tacking we get farther than others under full sail and oar — and it's a real feeling of one's own worth to keep up with the rest, or even pull ahead.
November 26.

I'm beginning, all things considered, to settle in here tolerably well. The best of it is that there's enough to do; and the crowd of people, all the new faces, make a colorful play before my soul. I've made the acquaintance of Count C—, a man I respect more with every day — a wide, clear mind that, just because it sees so much, is not for that reason cold, but radiates so much friendship and love. He took an interest in me when I had some business to settle with him and noticed, at the first words, that we understood each other, that he could talk with me as he can't with everyone. And I can't praise enough his open way with me. There's no joy in the world so warm, so deep, as the sight of a great soul opening itself to you.

chapters.title: December 24, 1771
paragraphs: Just as I foresaw, the ambassador gives me no end of vexation. He's the most punctilious fool you can imagine, one step at a time, finicky as an old maid — a man never satisfied with himself, whom no one can ever satisfy. I like to work briskly and let a thing stand once it's done; but he can hand me back a paper and say, "It's good, but look it over again — one can always find a better word, a neater particle." Then I could go to the devil. Not an "and," not the least little conjunction may be left out, and he's the sworn enemy of all the inversions that sometimes slip from my pen; if you don't reel off your sentence to the official tune, he can't make head or tail of it. It's misery to work with a man like that.

The one thing that makes up for it is Count C—'s confidence. He told me quite frankly the other day how dissatisfied he is with the slowness and fussiness of my ambassador. "People like that make life hard for themselves and everyone else. Still," he said, "you have to resign yourself to it, like a traveler who has to cross a mountain — of course, if the mountain weren't there the road would be much shorter and easier; but there it is, and over it he must go."

The old man can feel the count's preference for me over him, and it galls him, and he seizes every chance to run the count down in front of me. I stand up for the count, naturally, and that only makes things worse. Yesterday he got me really angry, for he meant me too: "Oh, the count gets on well enough with the world's business; he works easily, has a ready pen; but he's short on real scholarship, like all your literary types." He had a look on his face as if to say, "Did you feel that?" But it had no such effect on me; I despise a man who can think and behave that way. I stood my ground and fought back rather hotly. The count, I said, was a man you had to respect for his character as much as for his learning. "I've never known anyone," I said, "who has so succeeded in opening his mind to all sorts of subjects and yet keeping it active for everyday life." That was all Greek to the old man's brain, and I took my leave so as not to swallow more bile over some fresh absurdity.

And the fault is all yours — you who talked me into this harness with your sermons about being active. Activity! If the man who plants potatoes and rides into town to sell his grain isn't doing more than I am, then I'll gladly slave another ten years at the galley I'm chained to now.

And the glittering misery, the boredom, among the dreary people thrown together here! Their hunger for rank, the way they watch and lie in wait for the least step ahead of one another; the pettiest, most wretched passions, utterly naked. There's a woman, for instance, who bends everyone's ear about her noble birth and her lands, so that any stranger must think her a fool, puffed up over the bit of nobility and the name of her estate — when in fact she's nothing more than the daughter of a local clerk. You see, I can't make sense of a race of people who debase themselves so shamelessly.

Of course I see more clearly every day, dear friend, how foolish it is to judge others by oneself. And because I have so much to do with myself, and this heart of mine is so stormy — ah, I'd gladly let others go their own way, if only they'd let me go mine.

What annoys me most are the wretched social distinctions. I know as well as anyone how necessary differences of rank are, how many advantages they bring me myself; only let them not stand in my way just where I might still taste a little joy, a glimmer of happiness on this earth.

Lately, out walking, I made the acquaintance of a Miss B—, a charming creature who has kept much of her naturalness in the midst of all this stiff life. We took to each other in conversation, and when I left I asked leave to call on her. She granted it so frankly that I could hardly wait for the proper hour to go. She isn't from here, and lives with an aunt. The old woman's face I didn't like. I paid her a great deal of attention, addressed most of my talk to her, and in less than half an hour had pretty well guessed what the young lady afterward admitted to me herself: that her dear aunt, lacking everything in her old age — no decent fortune, no wit, and no support but the line of her ancestors, no shelter but the rank she's barricaded herself behind, and no pleasure but looking down from her upper floor over the heads of the townsfolk. She's said to have been beautiful in her youth, and to have frittered it away tormenting many a poor young fellow with her moods, and in her riper years bowed under the rule of an old officer who, for that price and a tolerable income, served out her brazen years with her and then died. Now in her iron years she's alone, and no one would so much as look at her, if her niece weren't so lovely.

chapters.title: January 8, 1772
paragraphs: What sort of people are these, whose whole soul hangs on ceremony, whose every thought and effort for years on end is bent on shoving themselves one chair higher up the table! Not that they've nothing else to do — no, the work piles up precisely because these petty vexations keep them from getting on with what matters. Last week, on a sleighing party, there was a quarrel over precedence, and the whole pleasure was ruined.

The fools, who can't see that place is really nothing, and that the man in the first place hardly ever plays the first part! How many kings are ruled by their ministers, how many ministers by their secretaries? And who, then, is first? The one, it seems to me, who sees through the rest and has power or cunning enough to harness their strength and their passions to carrying out his own plans.

chapters.title: January 20, 1772
paragraphs: I have to write to you from here, dear Charlotte, from the little room of a country inn where I've taken shelter from a hard storm. The whole time in that dismal hole of a town, D—, among people foreign — wholly foreign — to my heart, I never once felt a moment when my heart told me to write to you; but here, in this hut, in this seclusion, in this confinement, while the snow and sleet beat against my little window, here you were my first thought. The moment I stepped in, your image rose before me, your memory — oh, Charlotte, so holy, so warm! Good God, the first happy moment back again!

If you could see me, dear Charlotte, in this stream of distraction! How dried-up my senses are; not one full moment of the heart, not one blessed hour! Nothing! I stand as if before a peep-show and watch the little men and horses jerk past me, and often ask myself whether it isn't a trick of the eye. I play along, or rather I'm played with like a puppet, and sometimes take my neighbor by his wooden hand and start back with a shudder. In the evening I resolve to enjoy the sunrise, and don't get out of bed; by day I promise myself the moonlight, and stay in my room. I don't rightly know why I get up, why I lie down.
The leaven that drove my life is gone; the spell that kept me awake deep in the night, that woke me from my sleep in the morning, is gone.

I've found only one woman here, a Miss B—. She's like you, Charlotte — if anyone can be like you. "Well," you'll say, "the man's taken to paying pretty compliments!" There's something in it. For a while now I've been very charming, because I can't be otherwise; I'm full of wit, and the ladies say no one can praise so neatly — "or lie so well," you'll add, for the two go together, don't they? But I was speaking of Miss B—. She has a great deal of soul, which looks straight out of her full blue eyes. Her rank is a burden to her, satisfying none of the wishes of her heart. She longs to be out of all this turmoil, and we dream away many an hour together in the country, in scenes of unclouded happiness — and of you! How often she has to do you homage; has to, no — does it of her own accord, loves to hear about you, loves you.

Oh, that I were sitting at your feet in that dear, familiar little room, with our little ones tumbling around me! And if they got too loud for you, I'd gather them about me and quiet them with some hair-raising fairy tale. The sun is going down in glory over the snow-covered country; the storm has blown itself out; and I — must shut myself up again in my cage. Adieu! Is Albert with you? And how — ? God forgive me the question!

chapters.title: February 8, 1772
paragraphs: For a week now we've had the foulest weather, and it does me good. For as long as I've been here, no fine day has dawned in the sky without someone spoiling it for me or stealing it from me. When it really pours and sleets and freezes and blows — ha, I think, it can't be worse indoors than out, or the other way round — and so it's well. When the sun rises in the morning and promises a fine day, I can never keep from crying out, "There's another gift from heaven they can ruin for each other! There's nothing they don't ruin — health, good name, joy, rest! And mostly out of foolishness, dullness, and narrowness, and, to hear them tell it, with the best of intentions." Sometimes I could go down on my knees and beg them not to rage so against their own guts.

chapters.title: February 17, 1772
paragraphs: I'm afraid my ambassador and I won't last much longer together. The man is simply unbearable. His way of working and doing business is so ridiculous that I can't help contradicting him and often handling things my own way, after my own head — which of course never suits him. So he complained of me at court, and the minister gave me a reprimand — a mild one, to be sure, but a reprimand all the same — and I was on the point of resigning, when I got a private letter from him, a letter I knelt to in spirit before the high, noble, wise mind behind it. The way he scolds my too-keen sensitivity, the way he honors my overheated notions of effectiveness, of influence on others, of getting things done, as the high spirits of youth — not trying to crush them, only to soften them and steer them where they can really play their part and do real good. So now I'm braced again for a week, and at peace with myself. Peace of soul is a precious thing, and joy in oneself. Dear friend, if only the jewel weren't as brittle as it is beautiful and dear!

chapters.title: February 20, 1772
paragraphs: God bless you, my dear ones, and give you all the good days he keeps from me!

Thank you, Albert, for fooling me. I was waiting for word of when your wedding would be, and meant on that very day, with all ceremony, to take Charlotte's silhouette down from the wall and bury it among my other papers. Now you're a pair, and her picture is still here. Well, let it stay! And why not? I know I'm still with you, still in Charlotte's heart, without doing you any harm — I have the second place there, and I mean to keep it, I must keep it. Oh, I'd run mad if she could forget — Albert, there's hell in the thought. Albert, farewell! Farewell, angel of heaven! Farewell, Charlotte!

chapters.title: March 15, 1772
paragraphs: I've had an annoyance that will drive me from here. I gnash my teeth! Devil take it! It can't be undone, and you alone are to blame, you who spurred and goaded and tormented me into taking a post that wasn't made for me. Now I have it! Now you have it! And so you won't tell me again that my wild notions ruin everything, here, dear sir, is a plain account, clean and clear, the way a chronicler would set it down.

Count O— likes me, singles me out — you know that, I've told you a hundred times. Yesterday I dined with him, on the very day his grand company of lords and ladies gathers at his house in the evening, which I never gave a thought to, and it never struck me that we underlings don't belong there. Good. I dine with the count, and after dinner we walk up and down the great hall; I talk with him, with Colonel B— who joins us, and so the hour for the party comes on. God knows, I'm thinking of nothing. In sweeps the more-than-gracious Lady von S— with her lord and her well-hatched little gosling of a daughter, with her flat chest and trim little waist; in passing they make their high-born eyes and nostrils at me in the old approved style. And since I heartily detest the whole tribe, I was just about to take my leave, only waiting for the count to be free of their wretched chatter, when my Miss B— came in. As my heart always lifts a little at the sight of her, I stayed on, stood behind her chair, and only after a while noticed that she was talking to me with less than her usual openness, a little flustered. It struck me. Is she like all the rest? I thought, and was stung, and meant to go — and yet stayed, because I wanted to excuse her, and didn't believe it, and still hoped for a kind word from her, and — whatever you like. Meanwhile the room filled up. Baron F— in a whole wardrobe inherited from the coronation of Francis I; the court councillor R—, with his deaf wife; the shabbily turned-out J—, patching the gaps of his old-fashioned coat with new bits. They came in droves, and I talked with a few of my acquaintances, who were all very curt. I was thinking — and only had eyes for my Miss B—. I didn't notice the women whispering at the far end of the room, that it spread to the men, that Frau von S— spoke to the count (Miss B— told me all this afterward), until at last the count came up to me and drew me over to a window. "You know our odd ways," he said. "The company, I notice, is displeased to see you here. I wouldn't for the world —" "Your Excellency," I broke in, "I beg your pardon a thousand times; I should have thought of it sooner, and I know you'll forgive me this inconsistency. I meant to take my leave a while ago; an evil genius held me back," I added with a smile, and bowed. The count pressed my hand with a feeling that said everything. I slipped quietly out of the grand company, got into a carriage, and drove to M—, to watch the sunset from the hill there and read in my Homer the glorious canto where Ulysses is entertained by the noble swineherd. That was good.

In the evening I came back to supper. Only a few were still in the room, dicing in a corner with the cloth turned back. Then the good A— came in, laid down his hat when he saw me, came up to me and said softly, "You've had trouble?" "I?" I said. "The count sent you out of the party." "The devil take the party," I said. "I was glad to get into the open air." "Good," he said, "that you take it lightly. Only it vexes me that it's already all over the place." Now the thing began to gnaw at me. Everyone who came to table and looked at me — I imagined it was because of that. It made my blood boil.

And now, when wherever I go I'm pitied, when I hear my enviers crowing — There, you see what comes of conceited heads who plume themselves on their little wit and think they may flout every convention! — and more such kennel-talk — then I could drive a knife into my heart.

Say what you will about a man standing on his own feet — show me the one who can bear to have scoundrels run him down when they've got the better of him. When their gossip is empty, ah, then you can let it pass.
March 16.

Everything's after me. Today I met Miss B— out walking; I couldn't help speaking to her, and as soon as we were a little away from the others I told her how hurt I'd been by her manner the other day. "Oh, Werther," she said warmly, "how could you read my confusion that way, you who know my heart? What I suffered for you, from the moment I stepped into the room! I saw it all coming; a hundred times it was on the tip of my tongue to warn you. I knew the von S—s and the von T—s would sooner leave with their husbands than stay in your company; I knew the count couldn't afford to break with them — and now this fuss!" "What do you mean?" I said, hiding my fright — for everything Adelin had told me the day before ran like boiling water through my veins in that instant. "What it has already cost me!" said the sweet creature, with tears in her eyes. I was no longer master of myself, ready to throw myself at her feet. "Tell me what you mean!" I cried. The tears ran down her cheeks; I was beside myself. She wiped them away without trying to hide them. "You know my aunt," she began. "She was there and saw it all — with what eyes, Werther! Last night, and this morning, I've had to hear a sermon about my acquaintance with you, sit there and listen to you belittled and run down, and could not — dared not — defend you fully."

Every word she spoke went through my heart like a sword. She never felt what a mercy it would have been to keep it all from me; and on top of it she told me what else would be said about it, how the spiteful would gloat. How they'd revel in my comeuppance, my humbling, for the pride and contempt of others they've so often thrown in my face. To hear all that, Wilhelm, from her, in a voice of the truest sympathy — I was shattered, and I'm still raging inside. I wish someone would dare to throw it in my face, so I could run him through the body; the sight of blood would do me good. Oh, a hundred times I've taken up a knife to give my choked heart air. They tell of a noble breed of horses that, when they're driven too hard and run hot, bite open one of their own veins by instinct, to breathe. I often feel the same: I'd like to open a vein and win myself everlasting freedom.

chapters.title: March 24, 1772
paragraphs: I've sent in my resignation to the court, and I hope it will be accepted; forgive me for not asking your leave first. I have to get away, and I know all you'll say to talk me into staying, so — sweeten it for my mother. I can't help myself, so she'll have to put up with my not being able to help her either. It will hurt her, of course, to see the fine career her son had begun — privy councillor, ambassador, and who knows what — pulled up short, and the little horse stabled again. Make of it what you will, reckon up all the ways and means by which I might have stayed: enough, I'm going. But so you'll know where I'm bound — there's a Prince of —— here who has taken a great liking to my company; when he heard of my plans he asked me to come with him to his estates and spend the lovely spring there. I'm to be left entirely to myself, he promises, and since the two of us understand each other up to a point, I'll chance it and go with him.

chapters.title: April 19, 1772
paragraphs: Thank you for both your letters. I didn't answer because I left this sheet lying until my discharge should come through from the court; I was afraid my mother might turn to the minister and make my plan harder. But now it's done, my discharge has come. I won't tell you how reluctantly they granted it, nor what the minister wrote — you'd only start your lamenting again. The crown prince has sent me a parting gift of twenty-five ducats, with a word that moved me to tears; so I won't need the money from my mother that I asked for lately.

chapters.title: May 5, 1772
paragraphs: I leave here tomorrow, and since my birthplace lies only six miles off the road, I want to see it again, to remember the old days and their dreams. I'll go in by the same gate my mother drove out of with me when, after my father's death, she left the dear, familiar place to shut herself up in her unbearable town. Adieu, Wilhelm; you'll hear how the journey goes.

chapters.title: May 9, 1772
paragraphs: I've made the pilgrimage to my birthplace with all a pilgrim's reverence, and many an unlooked-for feeling took hold of me. By the great linden that stands a quarter-hour from the town on the way to S—, I had the carriage stop, got down, and sent it on, so as to go on foot and taste every memory new and warm and to my heart's content. There I stood under the linden that was once, when I was a boy, the goal and the boundary of my walks. How different now! Then, in happy ignorance, I longed out into the unknown world, where I hoped to find such nourishment, such delight for my heart, to fill and satisfy its stirring, hungry yearning. Now I come back from that wide world — oh, my friend, with how many shattered hopes, how many ruined plans!

I saw the mountains lying before me that had been the goal of my longing a thousand times. I used to sit here for hours, straining toward them, losing myself heart and soul in the woods and valleys that lay there so sweetly, half-hid, before my fond eyes — and then, when the hour came to turn back, with what reluctance I left this dear spot! I came up to the town; I greeted all the old, familiar little garden houses, and disliked the new ones, and all the other changes that had been made. I went in through the gate, and at once knew myself again completely. Dear friend, I won't go into the details; charming as it all was to me, it would grow dull in the telling. I had decided to lodge in the marketplace, right beside our old house. On my way I noticed that the schoolroom where a good old woman had penned up our childhood has been turned into a shop. I remembered the restlessness, the tears, the dullness of mind, the cramped heart, I suffered in that hole. I couldn't take a step that wasn't remarkable. A pilgrim in the Holy Land doesn't pass so many spots of sacred memory, and his soul is hardly fuller of holy stirrings. One more thing, to stand for a thousand: I went down along the river to a certain farmhouse — that used to be my walk too — to the little places where we boys practiced making the flattest stones skip the most times across the water. I remembered so vividly how I'd sometimes stand and watch the water, with what wondering presentiments I followed it, how marvelously I pictured the regions it was flowing to, and how soon I found the limits of my imagining — and yet it had to go on, and on, until I lost myself altogether in the sight of an invisible distance. There, my friend, just so hemmed in and just so happy were our glorious forefathers; so childlike their feeling, their poetry. When Ulysses speaks of the immeasurable sea and the boundless earth, it's so true, so human, so heartfelt, so narrow and mysterious. What good does it do me now that I can repeat with any schoolboy that the earth is round? A man needs only a few clods to be happy on, and fewer still to lie under.

I'm at the prince's hunting lodge now. He's a man you can live with easily, open and plain. Only there are strange creatures around him whom I can't make out at all. They don't seem to be rogues, and yet they haven't the look of honest men either. Sometimes they seem honest to me, and still I can't trust them. What grieves me is to hear him talk of things he's only read or heard about, and always from the same angle some other man has shown them to him.

And he values my mind and my talents more than this heart of mine, which after all is my one pride, the sole source of everything — all strength, all happiness, all misery. Ah, what I know, anyone can know; my heart is mine alone.

chapters.title: May 25, 1772
paragraphs: I had something in my head I didn't mean to tell you about until it was done; now that nothing's come of it, it's all one. I wanted to go to the wars; I've had it at heart a long time. That, above all, was why I followed the prince here — he's a general in ——'s service. On one of our walks I let my plan slip; he advised against it, and I'd have had to be more stubborn than sensible not to give way to his reasons.

chapters.title: June 11, 1772
paragraphs: Say what you like, I can't stay here any longer. What's the use? Time drags on me. The prince treats me as well as anyone could, and yet I'm not in my own element. At bottom we have nothing in common. He's a man of understanding, but of the most ordinary kind; his company gives me no more than reading a well-written book. I'll stay another week, and then off into the blue again. The best thing I've done here is my drawing. The prince has a feeling for art, and would feel it more keenly if he weren't fenced in by his wretched scholarship and the usual jargon. Many a time I grind my teeth when, with a warm imagination, I lead him through nature and art, and he, thinking to do wonderfully well, suddenly spoils it all by blundering in with some stock art-term.

chapters.title: July 16, 1772
paragraphs: Once more I'm a wanderer on the earth, a pilgrim. And what else are you all!

chapters.title: July 18, 1772
paragraphs: Where am I bound? I'll tell you in confidence. I have to stay here another two weeks, and then I've persuaded myself I want to visit the mines in ——. But really there's nothing in it; I only want to be near Charlotte again, that's all. And I laugh at my own heart — and do as it bids.

chapters.title: July 29, 1772
paragraphs: No, it's well! All is well! I — her husband! O God who made me, had you kept that happiness for me, my whole life would be one long prayer. I won't quarrel with you — forgive me these tears, forgive me these vain wishes. She, my wife! To have folded the dearest creature under the sun in my arms — A shudder runs through me, Wilhelm, from head to foot, when Albert puts his arm around her slim waist.

And — may I say it? Why not, Wilhelm? She would have been happier with me than with him! Oh, he's not the man to fill every wish of that heart. A certain want of feeling, a want — take it as you will — his heart doesn't beat in time with hers at — oh! — at some passage in a favorite book, where my heart and Charlotte's meet as one, and in a hundred other moments when it comes out, how we feel about something a third person has done. Dear Wilhelm! — true, he loves her with his whole soul, and what doesn't a love like that deserve!
An unbearable visitor has broken in on me. I've dried my tears. My thoughts have scattered. Adieu, dear friend!

chapters.title: August 4, 1772
paragraphs: I'm not the only one it goes so with. All men are cheated in their hopes, deceived in their expectations. I went to see my good woman under the lindens. The eldest boy ran to meet me; his shout of joy brought out his mother, and she looked very downcast. Her first word was: "Good sir, my little Hans is gone, alas!" — the youngest of her boys. I said nothing. "And my husband," she said, "is back from Switzerland with nothing; if some good people hadn't helped him, he'd have had to beg his way home. He caught a fever on the road." I could say nothing, and gave the little one something; she asked me to take a few apples, which I did, and left the place with a heavy heart.

chapters.title: August 21, 1772
paragraphs: My feelings shift from hour to hour. Sometimes a glad glimpse of life wants to open before me again — alas, only for a moment! When I lose myself this way in dreams, I can't help thinking: what if Albert were to die? Then you would — yes, she would — and then I chase the will-o'-the-wisp until it leads me to abysses I shrink back from in horror.

When I go out through the gate, along the road I first drove out by to fetch Charlotte for the ball, how wholly other it all is! Everything, everything is gone by. Not a hint of the world that was, not one pulse of my old feeling. I feel like a ghost coming back to the burnt-out, ruined castle that he built as a flourishing prince, fitting it out with every splendor, and left, full of hope, to a beloved son.

chapters.title: September 3, 1772
paragraphs: Sometimes I can't grasp it — that another can love her, may love her, when I love her so wholly, so deeply, so utterly, and know nothing, have nothing, am nothing but her!

chapters.title: September 4, 1772
paragraphs: Yes, so it is. As nature tips toward autumn, autumn comes in me and around me. My leaves are yellowing, and the leaves of the trees nearby have already fallen. Didn't I write to you, when I first came here, about a peasant lad? I asked after him again now in Walheim; they said he'd been turned out of his place, and no one would tell me more. Yesterday I met him on the road to another village; I spoke to him, and he told me his story, which moved me doubly and triply, as you'll easily understand when I tell it to you. But what's the use — why don't I keep what frightens and hurts me to myself? Why do I sadden you too? Why do I keep giving you cause to pity me and scold me? No matter — that too belongs to my fate.

At first the man answered my questions with a quiet sadness that seemed to me a little shy; but soon, as if he'd suddenly recognized himself and me again, more openly he confessed his faults and lamented his misfortune. Dear friend, if only I could put every word of his before you for judgment! He told me, owned to me, even with a kind of relish and happiness in the remembering, that his passion for his mistress had grown in him from day to day, until at last he no longer knew what he was doing, what — as he put it — what to do with himself. He couldn't eat, couldn't drink, couldn't sleep; something choked his throat; he did what he wasn't to do, forgot what he was told; it was as if an evil spirit chased him, until one day, knowing she'd gone up to an upper room, he'd followed her — been drawn after her, rather. When she wouldn't listen to his pleading, he tried to take her by force; he doesn't know what came over him, and God is his witness that his intentions toward her were always honest, that he wished nothing more fervently than that she'd marry him and spend her life with him. When he'd talked a while, he began to stammer, like a man with something more to say he doesn't dare bring out; until at last, shyly, he confessed too what little intimacies she'd allowed him, what nearness she'd granted. He broke off two or three times, and swore again and again that he wasn't saying it to make her out bad, as he put it — that he loved and prized her as before, that it had never crossed his lips, and he was only telling me to show that he wasn't a man wholly turned upside-down and out of his mind. And here, dear friend, I take up the old song again that I'll sing forever: if only I could set the man before you as he stood before me, as he stands before me still! If only I could tell you everything right, so you'd feel how I take part, must take part, in his fate! But enough — since you know my own fate too, know me, you know all too well what draws me to every poor wretch, and to this one above all.

Reading this letter over, I see I've forgotten to tell the end of the story — but it's easily guessed. She held herself off from him; her brother stepped in, a man who'd long hated him and wanted him out of the house, afraid that a new marriage of his sister's would rob his own children of the inheritance they hope for from her, since she's childless; and this brother threw him out at last, and made such a noise about the whole thing that the woman couldn't have taken him back even if she'd wanted to. Now she's hired another man, and they say she's fallen out with her brother over him too, and people are sure she'll marry this one — and my lad swears he won't live to see it.
What I'm telling you is not overdone, not prettied up; I may even say I've told it weakly, weakly, and coarsened it by telling it in our decent, handed-down words.

So this love, this faithfulness, this passion is no poet's invention. It lives, it is there in its purest being among the class of people we call uneducated, call crude. We educated ones — miseducated into nothing! Read the story with reverence, I beg you. Today I'm calm, writing it down; you see by my hand that I'm not scrawling and smearing as usual. Read it, my dear, and remember as you do that it's the story of your friend too. Yes, so it has gone with me, so it will go; and I'm not half so brave, not half so resolute, as the poor wretch — whom I almost don't dare set beside myself.

chapters.title: September 5, 1772
paragraphs: She'd written a note to her husband in the country, where he's kept by business. It began, "Dearest, best, come back as soon as ever you can; I wait for you with a thousand joys." A friend who came in brought word that, for certain reasons, he couldn't be back so soon. The note was left lying, and that evening it fell into my hands. I read it and smiled; she asked why. "What a heavenly gift the imagination is," I cried, "that I could fancy for a moment this was written to me." She broke off, seemed displeased, and I fell silent.

chapters.title: September 6, 1772
paragraphs: It cost me a struggle, but at last I had to give up the plain blue coat I wore the first time I danced with Charlotte; toward the end it had got quite past wearing. But I've had one made exactly like it, collar and cuffs and all, and a yellow waistcoat and breeches to match.
It doesn't do quite the same, though. I don't know — I think in time I'll come to like it better.

chapters.title: September 12, 1772
paragraphs: She'd been away a few days to fetch Albert. Today I went into her room; she rose to meet me, and I kissed her hand with such joy.

A canary flew off the mirror and onto her shoulder. "A new friend," she said, and coaxed it onto her hand; "it's for the little ones. Look how sweet it is! When I give it bread it flutters its wings and pecks so prettily. And it kisses me — look!"
She held her mouth to the little creature, and it pressed against her sweet lips so eagerly, as if it could feel the bliss it touched.
"It shall kiss you too," she said, and held the bird across. Its little beak made the way from her mouth to mine, and the pecking touch was like a breath, a foretaste, of love's joy.
"Its kiss isn't quite without greed," I said; "it's hunting for food, and turns away unsatisfied from an empty caress."
"It eats out of my mouth, too," she said, and offered it a few crumbs from her lips, smiling out of all the joy of an innocent, sharing love.

I turned my face away. She shouldn't do it! Shouldn't fire my imagination with these pictures of heavenly innocence and bliss, shouldn't wake my heart out of the sleep into which the dullness of life sometimes lulls it! And why not? — She trusts me so! She knows how I love her!

chapters.title: September 15, 1772
paragraphs: It's enough to drive a man mad, Wilhelm, that there should be people without sense or feeling for the few things on earth that still have any worth. You remember the walnut trees I sat under with Charlotte at the good vicar's at St—, those glorious trees that, God knows, always filled my soul with the greatest delight! How homely they made the parsonage yard, how cool, and how splendid the branches were; and the memory going back to the good clergymen who planted them so many years ago. The schoolmaster often gave us one of their names, that he'd heard from his grandfather; a fine man he's said to have been, and his memory was always sacred to me under those trees. I tell you, the schoolmaster had tears in his eyes yesterday when we spoke of how they'd been cut down. Cut down! I could go mad, I could kill the dog that struck the first blow. I, who could grieve myself to death if a couple of such trees stood in my yard and one died of old age — I have to stand by and watch this. But there's one thing, dear friend — there is such a thing as human feeling! The whole village grumbles, and I hope the vicar's wife will feel in her butter and eggs and the rest of it what a wound she's dealt the place. For it was she — the new incumbent's wife (our old one has died too) — a lean, sickly thing with good reason to take no part in the world, since no one takes any part in her. A fool who fancies herself learned, dabbles in the canon, works away busily at the newfangled moral-critical reform of Christianity, and shrugs her shoulders at Lavater's raptures; her health quite broken, so that she has no joy in God's earth. Only such a creature could cut down my walnut trees. You see, I can't get over it! Just imagine: the falling leaves make her yard wet and moldy; the trees rob her of daylight; and when the nuts are ripe the boys throw stones at them, and it jars her nerves, disturbs her deep musings as she weighs Kennicott against Semler and Michaelis. When I saw how put out the people were, the old ones especially, I said, "Why did you let it happen?" "When the bailiff wants a thing, here in the country," they said, "what's to be done?" But one thing pleased me. The bailiff and the vicar, who meant at least to make something off his wife's whims — the trees were to be theirs — wanted to split the profit; but the treasury heard of it, said, "This way," and bought the trees, for it had an old claim to that bit of ground. Down they lie, sold. Oh, if I were the prince! I'd know what to do with the vicar's wife, the bailiff, and the treasury — prince! Ah, if I were prince, what would I care about the trees in my own land!

chapters.title: October 10, 1772
paragraphs: Just to look into her black eyes makes me well! And what galls me is that Albert doesn't seem as happy as he — hoped to be — as I — would have been — if — I'm no friend of these dashes, but here there's no other way to say it; and I think I've said it plainly enough.

chapters.title: October 12, 1772
paragraphs: Ossian has driven Homer out of my heart. What a world the glorious bard leads me into! To roam over the heath, the storm-wind raging around, leading the spirits of the fathers in the smoking mist by the dim light of the moon; to hear from the hills, half-drowned in the roar of the mountain torrent, the fading groans of the spirits in their caves, and the laments of the girl grieving herself to death by the four moss-grown, grassy stones of the hero, her beloved, fallen. Then I find him, the gray wandering bard, seeking on the wide heath the footprints of his fathers, and finding, alas, their gravestones, and looking up with a wail to the dear evening star that hides in the rolling sea, and the ages of the past wake to life in the hero's soul, when the kindly beam still lit the brave through their dangers, and the moon shone down on their garlanded, homecoming ship. When I read the deep grief on his brow, see the last forsaken, glorious one stagger weary toward the grave, drinking ever new, painful-glowing joys from the powerless presence of his dead, and looking down at the cold earth, at the tall waving grass, and crying: "The wanderer will come, will come, who knew me in my beauty, and ask, Where is the singer, Fingal's noble son? His step passes over my grave, and he asks for me in vain over the earth." Then, O friend, like a noble squire I'd draw the sword and free my prince at one stroke from the quivering torment of a slow-dying life — and send my own soul after the freed half-god.

chapters.title: October 19, 1772
paragraphs: Oh, this gap, this fearful gap I feel here in my breast! I often think: if you could just once, only once, press her to this heart, the whole gap would be filled.

chapters.title: October 26, 1772
paragraphs: Yes, it grows certain to me, dear friend, certain and ever more certain, that the being of a single creature counts for little, very little. A friend of Charlotte's came to see her, and I went into the next room to find a book, and couldn't read, and then took up a pen to write. I heard them talking softly; they were telling each other trifles, the town news: this one's getting married, that one is sick, very sick — "a dry cough, the bones standing out in her face, and fainting fits; I wouldn't give a penny for her life," said the one. "And N— is in a bad way too," said Charlotte. "He's all swollen up," said the other. And my lively imagination set me down at the bedside of these poor people; I saw them turn from life with all their reluctance, saw them — and Wilhelm, my little ladies talked of it exactly as one talks of a stranger's dying. And when I look around me and look around this room, and see Charlotte's clothes lying about, and Albert's papers, and the furniture I'm so at home with, even this inkwell, I think: see what you are to this house! All in all. Your friends honor you, you often make their joy, and it seems to your heart it couldn't beat without them — and yet — if you went now, if you left this circle — would they feel, and how long would they feel, the gap your loss tears in their fate? How long? Oh, man is so fleeting that even there, where he has the one sure sense of his own being, where he makes the one true mark — even in the memory, in the soul of those he loves — there too he must be blotted out, must vanish, and that so soon!

chapters.title: October 27, 1772
paragraphs: Often I could tear my own breast open and dash out my brains, that one man can be so little to another. Ah, the love, the joy, the warmth, the rapture I don't bring to it myself, another won't give me, and with a heart full of bliss I can't make a man happy who stands cold and powerless before me.

chapters.title: October 27 — Evening, 1772
paragraphs: I have so much, and the feeling for her swallows it all up; I have so much, and without her it all comes to nothing.

chapters.title: October 30, 1772
paragraphs: A hundred times now I've been on the point of throwing my arms around her. The great God knows what it is to see so much loveliness move about before you and not be allowed to reach for it; and reaching is the most natural drive in us. Don't children reach for everything that comes into their heads? — And I?

chapters.title: November 3, 1772
paragraphs: God knows, I lie down so often in bed with the wish, sometimes even the hope, never to wake again; and in the morning I open my eyes, see the sun again, and am wretched. Oh, that I could be moody, lay the blame on the weather, on a third person, on a failed undertaking — then the unbearable weight of discontent would lie only half on me. Woe is me! I feel too surely that the fault lies in me alone — not the fault, no! Enough that the wellspring of all misery is hidden in me, as the wellspring of all bliss once was. Am I not the same man who once swam in a fullness of feeling, who turned every step into a paradise, who had a heart big enough to take in all of loving nature? And this heart is dead now; no raptures flow from it any more; my eyes are dry, and my senses, no longer washed by refreshing tears, knot my brow with anxious furrows. I suffer much, for I've lost what was the one delight of my life — the holy, quickening power with which I made worlds around me; it's gone! When I look out my window now at the far hill, at how the morning sun breaks through the mist above it and lights up the still meadow-ground, and the gentle river winds toward me between its leafless willows — oh, when this glorious nature stands before me as stiff as a little lacquered picture, and all the bliss can't pump one drop of happiness out of my heart up into my brain, and the whole fellow stands before the face of God like a dried-up well, like a cracked bucket! How often I've thrown myself on the ground and begged God for tears, as a farmer begs for rain when the sky is brass above him and the earth around him is dying of thirst.

But, ah, I feel it — God doesn't give rain and sunshine to our stormy begging; and those old days, whose memory tortures me — why were they so blessed? Because I waited in patience for his spirit, and took the joy he poured over me with a whole, a thankfully whole heart.

chapters.title: November 8, 1772
paragraphs: She's reproached me for my excesses — ah, so sweetly! My excesses: that I let myself be led, sometimes, by a glass of wine, into drinking a bottle. "Don't," she said. "Think of Charlotte!" "Think!" I said. "Need you tell me to? I think — I don't think! You're always before my soul. Today I sat on the spot where you got down from the carriage the other day —" She changed the subject to keep me from going deeper. Dear friend, I'm done for! She can do with me what she likes.

chapters.title: November 15, 1772
paragraphs: Thank you, Wilhelm, for your warm heart, for your well-meant advice — and be easy. Let me bear it out; for all my weariness I have strength enough to see it through. I honor religion, you know that; I feel it's a staff for many a weary soul, refreshment for many a fainting one. Only — can it be, must it be, that for everyone? When you look at the great world, you see thousands for whom it wasn't, thousands for whom it never will be, whether it's preached to them or not — so must it be that for me? Doesn't God's own Son say that those will be around him whom the Father gave him? And what if I'm not given? What if the Father wants to keep me for himself, as my heart sometimes tells me? — I beg you, don't read this wrong; don't see mockery in these innocent words. It's my whole soul I lay open to you; otherwise I'd rather have kept silent — as I'd rather not waste a word on what no one knows any more about than I do. What is it, the lot of man, but to drink out his measure, to drain his cup to the dregs? And if the cup was too bitter on the lips of the God of heaven in his human body, why should I play the brave man and pretend it tastes sweet? And why should I be ashamed, in the terrible moment when my whole being trembles between being and not-being, when the past flashes like lightning over the dark gulf of the future and everything around me sinks and the world goes down with me? Isn't this the voice of the creature thrown back wholly on itself, failing itself, falling past all holding, groaning down into the depths — "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" And should I be ashamed of the word, should I dread the moment, when he couldn't escape it who rolls up the heavens like a cloth?

chapters.title: November 21, 1772
paragraphs: She doesn't see, doesn't feel, that she's brewing a poison that will be the ruin of me and of her; and I, with full pleasure, drain the cup she hands me to my destruction. What does it mean, that kind look she so often — often? no, not often, but now and then — gives me; the readiness with which she takes an involuntary show of my feeling; the pity for what I bear, written on her brow?

Yesterday, as I left, she gave me her hand and said, "Adieu, dear Werther!" Dear Werther! It was the first time she called me "dear," and it went through me to the marrow. I've said it over to myself a hundred times, and last night, going to bed and chattering all sorts of things to myself, I suddenly said, "Good night, dear Werther!" — and then had to laugh at my own self.

chapters.title: November 22, 1772
paragraphs: I can't pray, "Let her be mine!" — and yet she so often seems to be mine. I can't pray, "Give her to me!" — for she belongs to another. I make jokes around my pains; if I let myself go I could spin out a whole litany of opposites.

chapters.title: November 24, 1772
paragraphs: She feels what I suffer. Today her look went deep into my heart. I found her alone; I said nothing, and she looked at me. And I no longer saw in her the lovely beauty, no longer the gleam of her splendid spirit; all that had vanished before me. A far more glorious look worked on me, full of the deepest sympathy, the sweetest tenderness. Why couldn't I throw myself at her feet? Why couldn't I fall on her neck and answer with a thousand kisses? She took refuge at the piano and breathed out, in a soft, sweet voice, low melodies in time with her playing. Never have I seen her lips so lovely; it was as if they parted thirstily to drink in the sweet tones welling from the instrument, and only the secret echo sounded back from the pure mouth — ah, if only I could say it to you! I gave way, bowed down, and swore: never will I dare press a kiss on you, lips over which the spirits of heaven hover. And yet — I want to — ha! you see, it stands like a wall before my soul — this bliss — and then to perish, to atone for the sin — Sin?

chapters.title: November 26, 1772
paragraphs: Now and then I tell myself: your fate is unique; call the others happy — no one was ever so tormented. Then I read some poet of the old world, and it's as if I were looking into my own heart. I have so much to bear! Ah, have men before me been so wretched?

chapters.title: November 30, 1772
paragraphs: I'll never come to myself again! Wherever I turn I meet some sight that throws me off. Today! O fate! O human kind!

I went down by the water at noon; I had no appetite. Everything was bleak; a cold, wet west wind blew off the mountains, and gray rain-clouds drove into the valley. From a distance I saw a man in a shabby green coat scrambling among the rocks, who seemed to be looking for plants. As I came nearer and he turned at the sound, I saw a very interesting face, whose chief mark was a quiet sadness, but otherwise nothing but an honest, good nature; his black hair was pinned up in two rolls, the rest braided in a thick plait down his back. As his dress seemed to mark him a man of humble station, I thought he wouldn't take it amiss if I noticed what he was at, and so I asked what he was looking for. "I'm looking," he answered with a deep sigh, "for flowers — and find none." "But it isn't the season for them," I said, smiling. "There are so many flowers," he said, coming down to me. "In my garden there are roses and two kinds of honeysuckle, one my father gave me; they grow like weeds; I've been looking for them two days now and can't find them. Out here there are always flowers too, yellow and blue and red, and the centaury has a pretty little blossom. I can't find a one of them." I noticed something uncanny, and so asked, in a roundabout way, what he wanted the flowers for. A strange, twitching smile drew over his face. "If you won't give me away," he said, pressing a finger to his lips, "I promised my sweetheart a posy." "That's good of you," I said. "Oh," he said, "she has lots of other things; she's rich." "And still she likes your posy," I said. "Oh, she has jewels, and a crown!" "What's her name, then?" "If only the States-General would pay me," he answered, "I'd be a different man! Yes, there was once a time when I was so well off! Now it's all over with me. Now I'm —" A wet look up to heaven said all. "So you were happy?" I said. "Ah, I wish I were so again!" he said. "Then I felt so well, so glad, so light, like a fish in water!" "Heinrich!" cried an old woman coming up the path. "Heinrich, where are you hiding? We've looked all over for you; come and eat." "Is that your son?" I asked, going to her. "Yes, my poor son," she answered. "God has laid a heavy cross on me." "How long has he been like this?" I asked. "This quiet," she said, "he's only been half a year. Thank God he's got this far; before that he raged a whole year, lay chained in the madhouse. Now he does no one any harm, only he's always meddling with kings and emperors. He was such a good, quiet lad, who helped feed me, wrote a fine hand, and then all at once he turned melancholy, fell into a violent fever, from there into madness, and now he's as you see him. If I were to tell you, sir —" I cut short her flood and asked, "And what was that time he praises so, when he was so happy, so well off?" "The poor fool," she cried with a pitying smile, "he means the time he was out of his mind; he never stops praising it — the time he was in the madhouse and knew nothing of himself." It struck me like a thunderclap; I pressed a coin into her hand and hurried off.

"When you were happy!" I cried, walking fast toward town. "When you felt as well as a fish in water!" — God in heaven! Is it the lot of man to be happy only before he comes to his reason and after he loses it again? Wretched creature! — and yet how I envy your gloom, the bewilderment of your senses you're lost in! You go out, full of hope, to pick flowers for your queen — in winter — and grieve to find none, and can't understand why you find none. And I — I go out without hope, without aim, and come home as I went. You fancy what a man you'd be if the States-General paid you. Blessed creature, who can blame your lack of happiness on an earthly hindrance! You don't feel — don't feel — that your misery lies in your shattered heart, in your wrecked brain, and that all the kings on earth can't help you.

Let him die without comfort who mocks the sick man traveling to the farthest spring that will only worsen his disease and make his dying harder; who sets himself above the burdened heart that goes on pilgrimage to the Holy Sepulchre to be rid of its sins. Every step that cuts his bare soles on the untrodden road is a drop of balm for his frightened soul, and with every day's journey he bears he lies down lighter at heart, eased of many a torment. — And dare you call that delusion, you wordmen lolling on your cushions? — Delusion! O God, you see my tears! Did you have to make man poor enough without robbing him of the little trust in you, the trust in you, all-loving Father? For trust in a healing root, in the tears of the vine — what is that but trust in you, that you've laid the healing and easing power into everything around us, the power we need at every hour? Father, whom I don't know — Father who once filled my whole soul and has turned his face from me now — call me to you! Be silent no longer! Your silence won't hold back this thirsting soul. — Could a man, a father, be angry if his son came back to him unlooked-for, fell on his neck and cried, "I'm here again, my father! Don't be angry that I break off the journey I should, by your will, have borne out longer. The world is everywhere the same — toil and labor, reward and joy; but what's it to me? I'm only well where you are, and before your face I'll suffer and rejoice." — And you, dear heavenly Father, would you turn such a one away from you?

chapters.title: December 1, 1772
paragraphs: Wilhelm! the man I wrote you about, that happy-unhappy one, was a clerk to Charlotte's father, and a passion for her that he nursed, hid, and at last confessed, which got him turned out of his place — this drove him mad. Feel, in these dry words, what a wild state the story put me in when Albert told it to me, as calmly as you'll perhaps read it.

chapters.title: December 4, 1772
paragraphs: I beg you — you see, it's all up with me. I can't bear it any longer! Today I sat by her — sat, and she played on the piano, all manner of tunes, and such feeling in them! Such! such! What would you have? Her little sister dressed her doll on my knee. The tears came into my eyes. I bent down and her wedding ring caught my eye — my tears flowed — and all at once she struck up the old, heavenly-sweet melody, just like that, and through my soul went a stab of comfort, and the whole memory of the past, of the other times I'd heard the song, of the dark stretches between, the vexation, the dashed hopes, and then — I walked up and down the room, my heart smothering under the press of it. "For God's sake," I said, in a violent burst toward her, "for God's sake, stop!" She broke off and looked at me, fixed. "Werther," she said, with a smile that cut right through my soul, "Werther, you're very ill; the things you love disgust you. Go — I beg you — calm yourself." I tore myself from her, and — God, you see my misery, and you'll make an end of it.

chapters.title: December 6, 1772
paragraphs: How her shape pursues me! Waking and dreaming she fills my whole soul. Here, when I shut my eyes, here in my brow, where the inner sight gathers, her black eyes stand. Here! I can't put it into words for you. When I close my eyes, there they are: like a sea, like an abyss, they lie before me, in me, filling all the senses of my brow.

What is man, that praised half-god? Don't his powers fail him just where he needs them most? And whether he soars in joy or sinks in suffering, isn't he checked in both, brought back to the dull, cold consciousness just when he longed to lose himself in the fullness of the infinite?
